entries.title: Convulsive status epilepticus (adult)
keyNumbers: Midazolam: 10 mg IM once (>40 kg); 5 mg if 13–40 kg
Lorazepam: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose) at ≤2 mg/min; may repeat once in 5–10 min
Levetiracetam: 60 mg/kg IV over 10 min (max 4500 mg)
Fosphenytoin: 20 mg PE/kg IV single dose (max 1500 mg PE); ≤150 mg PE/min
Valproate: 40 mg/kg IV single dose (max 3000 mg)
presentation: Bilateral tonic-clonic activity ≥5 min, or recurrent seizures without return to baseline between them
Subtle/late convulsive SE: coma with minimal motor signs (eye deviation, nystagmoid jerks, facial or limb twitching) — needs EEG
definitions: Operational SE: ≥5 min continuous clinical and/or electrographic seizure, or recurrent seizures without recovery between (NCS 2012)
Refractory SE: clinical or electrographic seizures continue after an adequate benzodiazepine plus one second-line ASM (NCS 2012)
EEG: convulsive electroclinical SE = bilateral tonic-clonic electroclinical seizure ≥5 continuous min (ACNS 2021)

immediateActions.action: ABCs, O2, cardiac monitor, IV/IO access; note seizure onset time; fingerstick glucose
Glucose <60 mg/dL: thiamine 100 mg IV, then D50W 50 mL IV
One full-dose benzodiazepine: IM midazolam OR IV lorazepam OR IV diazepam; only lorazepam/diazepam may be repeated once
Still seizing: load ONE second-line ASM — levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate (equivalent in ESETT, ~50% success). Don't wait out the window
Refractory: intubate, anesthetic infusion with cEEG → see refractory-super-refractory-se
Start cEEG if not returning to baseline or ongoing seizures suspected (NCS 2012)

workup.test: BMP with Ca, Mg, phos; CBC; LFTs
ASM levels (phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, etc.)
notes: Low level suggests nonadherence; free phenytoin if hypoalbuminemic
Affects valproate choice; consider eclampsia if pregnant/postpartum
Post-convulsive lactic acidosis is common and usually self-limited
After stabilization
Don't delay empiric antimicrobials/acyclovir for LP

indication: Not back to baseline after motor activity stops
notes: Start within 1 h of suspected ongoing seizures (NCS 2012)
Peri-ictal DWI/FLAIR changes can mimic stroke or encephalitis

treatment.doseText: 10 mg IM once (>40 kg); 5 mg if 13–40 kg
notes: Best when no IV access; single dose (not repeated in AES algorithm)
evidenceNote: AES 2016: Level A; IM midazolam superior to IV lorazepam without established IV access (RAMPART)

treatment.doseText: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose) at ≤2 mg/min; may repeat once in 5–10 min
notes: Give the full weight-based dose; 2 mg increments are a common underdosing error

treatment.doseText: 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg/dose); may repeat once
notes: Short duration of action due to redistribution — second-line load still needed
evidenceNote: NCS 2012: 0.15 mg/kg up to 10 mg, ≤5 mg/min

treatment.doseText: 15 mg/kg IV single dose (AES, initial or second phase); NCS 2012: 20 mg/kg, may add 5–10 mg/kg; rate 50–100 mg/min
notes: Efficacious first-line but slower to give; also an AES second-line option if levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate unavailable
Respiratory depression and hypotension, especially after benzodiazepines
evidenceNote: AES 2016: Level A as initial therapy (alternative, not first choice); Level B as second-line

treatment.doseText: 60 mg/kg IV over 10 min (max 4500 mg)
notes: Few interactions; adjust maintenance for renal function
Single dose; 4500 mg max per AES 2016 algorithm (also ESETT). Patients >75 kg receive <60 mg/kg
evidenceNote: ESETT 2019 RCT: 47% success, no difference vs fosphenytoin or valproate

treatment.doseText: 20 mg PE/kg IV single dose (max 1500 mg PE); ≤150 mg PE/min. NCS: may add 5 mg PE/kg
notes: Cardiac monitoring: hypotension and arrhythmia with fast infusion
1500 mg PE max per AES 2016 algorithm (also ESETT); patients >75 kg receive <20 mg PE/kg
evidenceNote: AES 2016: Level U (predates ESETT); fosphenytoin preferred over phenytoin for tolerability (Level A)

treatment.doseText: 40 mg/kg IV single dose (max 3000 mg); NCS: 20–40 mg/kg at 3–6 mg/kg/min
notes: Avoid if pregnant/childbearing potential (when alternatives exist), hepatic disease, suspected mitochondrial disease (POLG), urea-cycle disorder
Carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem) sharply lower valproate levels — choose another ASM
Check ammonia if encephalopathic
evidenceNote: AES 2016: Level B (one class II study)

notes: PR prolongation/AV block — baseline ECG
No RCT in convulsive SE; RCT data are for NCS (TRENdS)
evidenceNote: NCS 2012 lists as urgent control option

treatment.doseText: See refractory-super-refractory-se
notes: Requires intubation and cEEG

pitfalls: Benzodiazepine underdosing is the most common error — one full weight-based dose, not small repeated doses
Algorithm windows are upper limits; load the second-line ASM as soon as benzodiazepines fail
Stopped jerking ≠ stopped seizing; persistent coma needs EEG to exclude NCSE
~9–11% of ESETT patients ultimately had psychogenic nonepileptic events — treat as SE, but reconsider if atypical (eyes forcibly closed, pelvic thrusting, waxing-waning)
Phenytoin/fosphenytoin are not effective for alcohol-withdrawal seizures
Meropenem/ertapenem + valproate = subtherapeutic valproate
escalateWhen: Seizures persist after benzodiazepine + one second-line ASM → ICU, intubation, anesthetic infusion, cEEG
Not back to baseline after motor activity stops → cEEG
Airway compromise, hypoxemia, or hemodynamic instability
New-onset refractory SE without a clear cause → NORSE pathway (immunotherapy within 72 h)
institutionVaries: Which second-line ASM is in ED/floor automated dispensing and premixed bag sizes
Whether undiluted IV-push levetiracetam is permitted

entries.title: Refractory & super-refractory status epilepticus (incl. NORSE)
keyNumbers: Midazolam: Load 0.2 mg/kg at 2 mg/min; maintain 0.05–2 mg/kg/h
Propofol: Load 1–2 mg/kg; start 20 mcg/kg/min; maintain 30–200 mcg/kg/min
PRIS risk: caution >80 mcg/kg/min for >48 h
Pentobarbital: Load 5–15 mg/kg at ≤50 mg/min (may add 5–10 mg/kg); maintain 0.5–5 mg/kg/h
Methylprednisolone (NORSE first-line immunotherapy): 20–30 mg/kg/day IV (max 1 g/day) ×3–5 days; start within 72 h
presentation: Ongoing clinical or electrographic seizures after benzodiazepine + one second-line ASM
Often intubated, minimal motor signs — EEG is the only reliable monitor
definitions: RSE: clinical or electrographic seizures continue after an adequate benzodiazepine plus one second-line ASM (NCS 2012)
SRSE: SE that continues or recurs ≥24 h after onset of anesthetic therapy, including recurrence on reduction or withdrawal of anesthesia (Shorvon & Ferlisi 2011)
NORSE: new-onset RSE without active epilepsy or other pre-existing relevant neurologic disorder, and without a clear acute or active structural, toxic, or metabolic cause (Hirsch 2018)
FIRES: NORSE subtype with a febrile infection starting 2 weeks to 24 h before RSE onset, ± fever at SE onset (Hirsch 2018)

immediateActions.action: ICU; intubate; arterial line; vasopressor ready
cEEG now (within 1 h of suspected ongoing SE)
Anesthetic infusion — propofol or midazolam (local first tier); titrate to electrographic seizure suppression
Maximize maintenance ASMs (≥1 additional agent) so the wean can succeed; correct metabolic/toxic drivers
Escalate to ketamine or pentobarbital (local second tier)
Slow wean of infusion under cEEG; re-escalate if seizures recur
NORSE: IV methylprednisolone first-line (IVIG alternative or concurrent); ketogenic diet in week 1; second-line immunotherapy within 7 days if inadequate response

notes: ≥24 h after seizure cessation and during weaning (NCS 2012)

workup.test: LP: cells, protein, glucose, culture, HSV/VZV PCR, IgG index, oligoclonal bands, autoimmune encephalitis panel
notes: Send serum AND CSF neural antibody panels

workup.test: Tumor screen: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; pelvic or testicular ultrasound
notes: Ovarian teratoma in NMDAR encephalitis
Propofol infusion syndrome surveillance

workup.test: ASM levels, tox screen, BMP/Mg/phos/Ca, LFTs, ammonia

treatment.doseText: Load 1–2 mg/kg; start 20 mcg/kg/min; maintain 30–200 mcg/kg/min. Breakthrough: ↑5–10 mcg/kg/min q5 min or 1 mg/kg bolus
notes: PRIS risk: caution >80 mcg/kg/min for >48 h (rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, renal and cardiac failure)
Hypotension, especially with loading dose
Adjust daily calories for lipid (1.1 kcal/mL)

treatment.doseText: Load 0.2 mg/kg at 2 mg/min; maintain 0.05–2 mg/kg/h. Breakthrough: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg bolus and ↑0.05–0.1 mg/kg/h q3–4 h
notes: Tachyphylaxis with prolonged use
Active metabolite renally eliminated — slow offset in renal failure; no propylene glycol

treatment.doseText: Infusion: mean 2.2 ± 1.8 mg/kg/h in the largest SRSE series (observed, not a target); prior series means 1.3–2.8 mg/kg/h, max reported 10.5 mg/kg/h. Bolus: no dose in this source — use local protocol
notes: Added to midazolam in all 68 patients of the Alkhachroum series
Associated with stable MAP and falling vasopressor needs; no ICP/CPP/CBF effect in the multimodal-monitoring subgroup
Response better when started earlier and at higher doses (retrospective)
evidenceNote: Alkhachroum 2020: retrospective, n=68; ≥50% seizure-burden reduction within 24 h in 81%

treatment.doseText: Load 5–15 mg/kg at ≤50 mg/min (may add 5–10 mg/kg); maintain 0.5–5 mg/kg/h. Breakthrough: 5 mg/kg bolus, ↑0.5–1 mg/kg/h q12h
notes: Hypotension, cardiac depression, paralytic ileus; infection risk
IV formulation contains propylene glycol
At high doses: complete loss of neurologic function — exam unreliable for days

treatment.agent: Maintenance ASMs (levetiracetam, lacosamide, valproate, phenobarbital, others)
treatment.doseText: Per agent; optimize before each wean attempt
notes: Phenobarbital maintenance can help wean anesthetics

treatment.doseText: 20–30 mg/kg/day IV (max 1 g/day) ×3–5 days; start within 72 h. Enteral steroids are not a substitute
notes: Steroids are the first-line immunotherapy; IVIG and steroids may be given simultaneously
Any adult ≥50 kg reaches the 1 g cap

treatment.doseText: 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days (e.g., 0.4 g/kg/day ×5)
notes: Alternative to, or concurrent with, steroids
PLEX: no consensus recommendation beyond not delaying other treatments; if used after IVIG it removes it

treatment.agent: Second-line immunotherapy (noninfectious NORSE, inadequate first-line response)
treatment.doseText: Choose by suspected etiology, start within 7 days: rituximab if pathogenic antibody identified/highly suspected; IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) or IL-6 blocker (tocilizumab) if cryptogenic without autoimmune-encephalitis features. Dose with neuroimmunology/pharmacy
notes: Plus ketogenic diet in the first week (parenteral if enteral not possible)
May still help when started weeks after onset

pitfalls: Paralytics stop motor signs, not seizures — cEEG is mandatory
EEG target (seizure suppression vs burst suppression) is not established — choose and document one
Breakthrough seizures during weaning are common — re-escalate and strengthen maintenance ASMs
Don't hold immunotherapy in cryptogenic NORSE for antibody results (send-outs take days to weeks)
Propofol infusion syndrome: rising lactate, CK, triglycerides, arrhythmia, acidosis
Cannabidiol and hypothermia are not first-line in NORSE (Wickström 2022)
escalateWhen: SRSE or NORSE → tertiary center with neuro-ICU, epilepsy, and neuroimmunology expertise (Wickström 2022)
Hemodynamic instability limiting anesthetic titration
No 24/7 cEEG reading locally
institutionVaries: Infusion order (local: propofol or midazolam → ketamine or pentobarbital)
EEG target and duration before wean
24/7 cEEG reading; ketogenic diet protocol availability
Dosing weight for infusions in obesity
Ketamine bolus dose (no consensus source)

entries.title: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus & ictal-interictal continuum
keyNumbers: Electrographic SE: electrographic seizure ≥10 continuous min, or >20% of any 60-min period (ACNS 2021)
Lorazepam: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose)
Lacosamide: 400 mg IV over 30 min (TRENdS); rebolus 200 mg for breakthrough; then 200 mg q12h
Fosphenytoin: 20 mg PE/kg IV (TRENdS infused ≤75 mg PE/min); rebolus 5 mg PE/kg
Levetiracetam: 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg)
presentation: Unexplained or fluctuating impaired consciousness, or failure to awaken after convulsive SE
Subtle signs: eye deviation, nystagmus, automatisms, facial/limb twitching, aphasia, perseveration
High-risk: acute brain injury, sepsis, renal failure on neurotoxic drugs, recent convulsive SE
definitions: Electrographic seizure: epileptiform discharges averaging >2.5 Hz for ≥10 s, OR any pattern with definite evolution lasting ≥10 s (ACNS 2021)
Electrographic SE: electrographic seizure ≥10 continuous min, or >20% of any 60-min period (ACNS 2021)
Electroclinical seizure: any pattern with a time-locked clinical correlate, OR EEG + clinical improvement with a parenteral ASM (ACNS 2021)
Electroclinical SE: ≥10 continuous min, or >20% of any 60 min; ≥5 min if bilateral tonic-clonic (ACNS 2021)
Possible ECSE: an IIC pattern ≥10 continuous min or >20% of any 60 min that improves on EEG with a parenteral ASM but without clinical improvement (ACNS 2021)

IIC: PDs/SW averaging >1.0 to <2.5 Hz over 10 s; OR >0.5 to <1 Hz with plus modifier or fluctuation; OR lateralized RDA >1 Hz for ≥10 s with plus modifier or fluctuation; and not an ESz/ESE (ACNS 2021)

immediateActions.action: Urgent EEG — cEEG preferred; a routine 20–30 min study can miss intermittent seizures
Correct glucose, Na, Ca, Mg; review neurotoxic drugs (cefepime in renal failure, ifosfamide, lithium)
Benzodiazepine (if not already given) + load a second-line ASM; lacosamide noninferior to fosphenytoin for NCS (TRENdS)
Parenteral ASM trial with serial exam + EEG (local protocol); EEG AND clinical improvement = ECSE; EEG-only improvement = possible ECSE
Weigh anesthetic infusion against harms; intensity depends on etiology, consciousness level, and comorbidity

notes: ≥48 h in comatose patients after acute brain insult (NCS 2012)

workup.test: BMP, Ca, Mg, phos, glucose, LFTs, ammonia

notes: Cefepime, ifosfamide, lithium, ASM levels
Peri-ictal cortical/pulvinar DWI changes can occur

treatment.doseText: As convulsive SE: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose)
notes: Watch airway in non-intubated patients

treatment.doseText: 400 mg IV over 30 min (TRENdS); rebolus 200 mg for breakthrough; then 200 mg q12h
notes: 400 mg load is above the FDA-labeled load (TRENdS ran under an IND)
PR prolongation — ECG; caution with AV block
evidenceNote: TRENdS 2018 RCT: noninferior to fosphenytoin (63% vs 50% seizure control)

treatment.doseText: 20 mg PE/kg IV (TRENdS infused ≤75 mg PE/min); rebolus 5 mg PE/kg
notes: Hypotension/arrhythmia; slower rate in older or cardiac patients

treatment.doseText: As convulsive SE: 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg)
As convulsive SE: 40 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg)
notes: Same contraindications as in convulsive SE (see that entry)

treatment.doseText: See refractory-super-refractory-se
notes: Reserve for refractory NCSE where benefit plausibly outweighs intubation/ICU harms

pitfalls: No convulsions ≠ no seizures — nonconvulsive seizures are common in ICU patients and invisible without EEG
GPDs with triphasic morphology in metabolic encephalopathy can mimic NCSE; a benzodiazepine trial may sedate without clarifying
Cefepime neurotoxicity in renal failure can cause or mimic NCSE — stop or renally dose it
Overtreatment is a real risk: anesthetic coma for non-comatose NCSE may cause more harm than benefit
escalateWhen: NCSE persisting after 2 ASMs → neuro-ICU discussion
No cEEG available locally and NCSE suspected → transfer
institutionVaries: cEEG availability and remote reading hours
Protocol and agent for the parenteral ASM/benzodiazepine trial

entries.title: Myasthenic crisis (impending and manifest)
keyNumbers: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30 cmH2O, or rapid decline (thresholds extrapolated from GBS)
Single breath count <20
IVIG: 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days (Gilhus 2024: over 3–5 consecutive days; e.g., 0.4 g/kg/day ×5)
Plasma exchange (PLEX): 1–1.5 total plasma volumes per exchange; 3–6 exchanges over 10–14 days (daily or alternate days); albumin replacement
presentation: Rapidly worsening bulbar weakness (dysphagia, nasal speech, weak cough, pooled secretions), neck flexor weakness, dyspnea/orthopnea
Limb weakness may be mild relative to respiratory/bulbar involvement
Triggers: infection, surgery, MG-worsening drugs, steroid start or taper, pregnancy/postpartum, immune checkpoint inhibitors
definitions: Impending crisis: rapid clinical worsening that, in the treating physician's opinion, could lead to crisis in days to weeks (ICG 2016)
Manifest crisis: worsening myasthenic weakness requiring intubation or NIV to avoid intubation, excluding routine postoperative use (ICG 2016)

immediateActions.action: Bedside respiratory set: FVC (mL/kg), NIF/MIP, single breath count, cough, secretions, neck flexion; repeat every few hours
Early signs of crisis → ICU admission (Gilhus 2024); at minimum close respiratory/bulbar monitoring for impending crisis (ICG 2016)
Low threshold for elective intubation; BiPAP trial reasonable before intubation if no significant hypercapnia or bulbar failure (hypercapnia predicts NIV failure)
Start IVIG (local default) or PLEX (available 24/7); favor PLEX for MuSK-MG or when fastest response needed
Stop MG-worsening drugs (see mg-contraindications); treat trigger
Corticosteroids: either start high dose alongside IVIG/PLEX (covers the steroid dip) or wait several days for IVIG/PLEX effect — both endorsed; see treatment
Stop pyridostigmine during crisis (secretions, airway plugging); restart before weaning from ventilation

notes: Facial weakness → poor seal; use face mask
Hypercapnia is late; a normal gas does not exclude impending failure

workup.test: Infection screen: CXR, UA, cultures as indicated
BMP with K, Mg, Ca, phos; CBC; TSH
Renal function and coagulation before IVIG/PLEX

notes: Screen for myositis/myocarditis overlap
If serostatus unknown; send before IVIG/PLEX
If not previously done

treatment.doseText: 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days (Gilhus 2024: over 3–5 consecutive days; e.g., 0.4 g/kg/day ×5)
notes: Caution: thrombosis risk, renal failure, volume overload, IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
Avoid in hypercoagulable states and renal failure (ICG 2016)
IVIG efficacy less certain in mild or ocular MG
Prolonged/severe crisis expected: sequential PLEX first, then IVIG, is superior (Gilhus 2024)
evidenceNote: ICG 2016: IVIG and PLEX probably equally effective in severe generalized MG
AAN 2012: IVIG effective in moderate–severe MG (Level B)
ASFA 2023: IVIG and TPE generally regarded as equally effective in acute MG
Gilhus 2024: PLEX and IVIG are the primary crisis treatments; choose by availability and patient factors

treatment.doseText: 1–1.5 total plasma volumes per exchange; 3–6 exchanges over 10–14 days (daily or alternate days); albumin replacement
notes: Effect within hours to days, lasts ~3–6 weeks — start/adjust immunosuppression
ASFA: TPE favored with severe respiratory impairment, and more effective if started early in the admission; may be more effective in MuSK-MG
Contraindicated in sepsis (ICG 2016); hypotension, citrate hypocalcemia, line complications
Don't give PLEX shortly after IVIG (removes it)
Meta-analysis: slightly higher response rate and faster improvement with PLEX (Gilhus 2024)
evidenceNote: ASFA 2023: Category I, Grade 1B (acute short-term treatment incl. crisis)
ICG 2016: expert consensus — PLEX faster and possibly more effective in crisis

treatment.agent: Already on a C5 inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan): supplemental dose with PLEX or IVIG
treatment.doseText: Eculizumab: after each PLEX session, 300 mg if the most recent dose was 300 mg, or 600 mg if it was ≥600 mg, within 60 min; acute-rescue IVIG needs no supplement. Ravulizumab: after each PLEX session, within 4 h — 40 to <60 kg: 1,200 mg (most recent dose 2,400 mg) or 1,500 mg (3,000 mg); 60 to <100 kg: 1,500 mg (2,700 mg) or 1,800 mg (3,300 mg); ≥100 kg: 1,500 mg (3,000 mg) or 1,800 mg (3,600 mg); after completing an IVIG cycle, 600 mg within 4 h. Zilucoplan: label gives no PLEX/IVIG guidance

dose.label: Eculizumab after PLEX (most recent dose 300 mg)
frequency: Within 60 min after each PLEX session

dose.label: Eculizumab after PLEX (most recent dose ≥600 mg)
frequency: Within 60 min after each PLEX session

dose.label: Ravulizumab after PLEX (by weight and most recent dose — see doseText)
frequency: Within 4 h after each PLEX session

dose.label: Ravulizumab after an IVIG cycle
frequency: Within 4 h after completing the IVIG cycle

notes: Eculizumab with scheduled (non-rescue) IVIG in gMG: 300 or 600 mg supplement by IVIG frequency and most recent dose (Soliris Table 3)
evidenceNote: Zilbrysq PI: no PLEX/IVIG statement; no drug-interaction section

treatment.agent: Already on an FcRn blocker (efgartigimod IV or SC, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab): IVIG, PLEX or a C5 inhibitor
treatment.doseText: No label dose adjustment or timing interval. Labels: FcRn blockers may lower exposure and reduce effectiveness of drugs that bind FcRn (IVIG, IgG monoclonal antibodies) — monitor for reduced effect
notes: Eculizumab and ravulizumab labels: FcRn blockers may lower their exposure — monitor for reduced effect
FcRn-blocker labels say nothing about PLEX
Active infection: labels say delay the FcRn-blocker dose; serious infection: consider withholding until resolved
Long-term need for an FcRn-binding drug: labels say consider stopping the FcRn blocker

treatment.agent: Prednisone / prednisolone (or IV methylprednisolone in ICU)
treatment.doseText: Moderate–severe gMG: 0.75–1.00 mg/kg/day PO. When rapid response needed: 30–50 mg daily from the start, combined with IVIG/PLEX. ICU add-on option: prednisone 3–4 mg/kg or IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/day (Gilhus 2024)
notes: Transient worsening within the first 2 weeks — why it is paired with IVIG/PLEX (ICG 2020; Gilhus 2024)
ICG 2016 alternative: wait several days for IVIG/PLEX effect before starting
The ICU 'very high dose' option (3–4 mg/kg prednisone, MP 500 mg/day) rests on a single cited reference in a position paper — confirm against local practice before use

treatment.doseText: Discontinue during crisis; restart before weaning from mechanical ventilation
notes: Increases airway secretions (ICG 2016)
True cholinergic crisis is rare — don't escalate pyridostigmine to treat crisis

treatment.agent: Aspiration precautions, NPO until swallow eval, chest physiotherapy
treatment.doseText: N/A

pitfalls: Vital capacity and blood gases do not reliably predict the need for ventilation (Gilhus 2024) — trend function and bulbar signs
SpO2 and ABG stay normal until late — trend FVC/NIF and bulbar function
Neck flexor weakness parallels diaphragm weakness
Steroid initiation can worsen MG in the first ~2 weeks
Common inpatient triggers: fluoroquinolones, macrolides, aminoglycosides, IV magnesium, beta-blockers, ICIs; use iodinated contrast cautiously
ICI-associated MG is often severe with high crisis rates (ICG 2020)
The 20/30/40 thresholds are borrowed from GBS cohorts; trajectory matters more than any single value

On a C5 inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan): signs of meningococcal infection → evaluate immediately, even if vaccinated (boxed warning); consider interrupting the drug during treatment of serious meningococcal infection
Meningococcal Patient Safety Card (REMS) is carried after stopping eculizumab (3 months), ravulizumab (8 months) or zilucoplan (2 months)
Rozanolixizumab: serious drug-induced aseptic meningitis reported — work up per standard care; trial headache 44%, pyrexia 17%
Inebilizumab (Uplizna, also gMG-indicated): label gives no PLEX/IVIG guidance
escalateWhen: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30 cmH2O, or rapid decline (thresholds extrapolated from GBS)
Unable to handle secretions, weak cough, or rising PaCO2
Single breath count <20
institutionVaries: IVIG product and dosing weight in obesity (actual vs adjusted)
PLEX access (peripheral vs central) and exchange schedule
Whether IgA level is checked before IVIG
Steroid strategy in crisis (concurrent high-dose start vs delayed start; ICU IV methylprednisolone use)
REMS: eculizumab and ravulizumab are dispensed only by REMS-certified healthcare settings and pharmacies — confirm before PLEX so the supplemental dose can be given

entries.title: Guillain-Barré syndrome
keyNumbers: IVIG: 0.4 g/kg/day IV ×5 days (2 g/kg total)
Plasma exchange (PLEX): 12–15 L total in 4–5 exchanges over 1–2 weeks (within 4 weeks of onset, unable to walk unaided); 2 exchanges if able to walk but not run (within 2 weeks)
Ward → ICU: FVC <60% predicted, SBC <20, autonomic instability, worsening bulbar/neck weakness, or mEGRIS ≥23 (EAN/PNS 2023 Fig. 2)
FVC fall >30% in 24 h → immediate ICU transfer; 50% fall in <24 h → likely needs ventilation
In ICU: FVC <20 mL/kg, MEP <30 cmH2O, MIP <40 cmH2O, or FVC >30% below baseline → consider elective intubation before FVC ≤10 mL/kg
presentation: Progressive bilateral limb weakness with reduced/absent reflexes; nadir within 4 weeks
Back/limb pain, distal paresthesias; facial or bulbar weakness; dysautonomia
Preceding diarrhea or respiratory infection makes GBS more likely
MFS: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia (anti-GQ1b)
definitions: Progressive worsening ≤4 weeks; progression >8 weeks from onset or ≥3 treatment-related fluctuations (TRFs) → consider acute-onset CIDP (EAN/PNS 2023)
TRF: worsening after initial treatment-induced improvement or stabilization (EAN/PNS 2023)
CSF: raised protein with normal or slightly raised cells — <5/μL in 80%, 5–50/μL in 19%, >50/μL in 2%; >50/μL → consider alternative diagnosis (EAN/PNS 2023)
GBS disability scale: 1 minor symptoms, can run; 2 walks 10 m unaided, can't run; 3 walks 10 m with aid; 4 bed/chair-bound; 5 ventilated; 6 dead
CSF protein raised in 50% at <3 days and 84% at >7 days from onset (EAN/PNS 2023, n>1000)

High risk at presentation (→ ICU): mEGRIS 25–32 (>70% ventilation risk), OR ≥4 of 6 risk factors (<7 days onset→admission, can't cough, GBS-DS ≥4, can't lift arm above horizontal, neck flexion weakness, abnormal LFTs), OR FVC <60% predicted / aspiration risk / autonomic instability (EAN/PNS 2023 Fig. 2)
Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis: MFS features plus impaired consciousness and pyramidal signs, often overlapping with GBS; IgG anti-GQ1b/GT1a (Leonhard 2019; Willison & Yuki 2002)

immediateActions.action: FVC, single breath count, MIP/MEP if available; bulbar and neck flexion strength. FVC 3–6×/day (q4h while falling)
Continuous ECG and frequent BP — screen for dysautonomia
Risk-stratify (definitions): high risk → ICU. Ward patients: transfer to ICU if FVC <60% predicted, SBC <20, autonomic instability, clinical deterioration (esp. bulbar/neck), or mEGRIS ≥23
Unable to walk unaided: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day ×5 (local first choice) or PLEX 12–15 L over 4–5 exchanges (≤4 weeks)
VTE prophylaxis, pain control, bowel/bladder care, swallow eval, early PT/OT

notes: Protein often normal in week 1 — doesn't exclude GBS
IVIG can raise CSF protein and cells; tap before IVIG if possible
Can be normal early; repeat if nondiagnostic

workup.test: BMP (K, Mg, phos), CK, CBC, LFTs, glucose
notes: Abnormal LFTs at presentation raise ventilation risk

workup.test: Contrast MRI of the whole spine
notes: Excludes cord compression, myelitis, tumor; root enhancement supports GBS
Anti-ganglioside panels of limited value in typical GBS; assay-dependent; a negative result doesn't exclude GBS (Leonhard 2019)

indication: Suspected autoimmune nodopathy (severe, tremor, poor IVIG response)

workup.test: HIV, Lyme, CMV, West Nile serology/PCR

treatment.doseText: 0.4 g/kg/day IV ×5 days (2 g/kg total)
notes: 2-day 1 g/kg/day regimen not endorsed (more TRFs in a pediatric trial)
Also reasonable 2–4 weeks after onset (GPP)
evidenceNote: EAN/PNS 2023: strong recommendation if unable to walk unaided within 2 weeks of onset

treatment.doseText: 12–15 L total in 4–5 exchanges over 1–2 weeks (within 4 weeks of onset, unable to walk unaided); 2 exchanges if able to walk but not run (within 2 weeks)
notes: Albumin replacement preferred (FFP: similar outcome, more adverse events)
Discontinuous-flow machines relatively contraindicated with severe dysautonomia
evidenceNote: EAN/PNS 2023: strong recommendation (4–5 exchanges); weak recommendation (2 exchanges, mild)

treatment.agent: Neuropathic pain: gabapentinoid, tricyclic, or carbamazepine
treatment.doseText: Per agent; titrate
notes: Caution with tricyclics in autonomic failure

treatment.doseText: Per institutional protocol for non-ambulatory patients
Do not use
evidenceNote: EAN/PNS 2023: recommends against oral steroids (strong); weak recommendation against IV steroids

treatment.agent: Second IVIG course (poor prognosis) / PLEX followed immediately by IVIG
treatment.doseText: Do not use
notes: SID-GBS: second course added no benefit, more thromboembolic events
Retreatment for a TRF may be considered (observational data only)

pitfalls: Normal CSF protein in the first week is common
CSF cells >50/μL → think infection (HIV, Lyme, CMV, West Nile), malignancy, sarcoid
Sensory level, extensor plantars, or early sphincter dysfunction → image the cord
Severe respiratory failure with only mild limb weakness → reconsider diagnosis (MG, botulism, myopathy)
Mild stable GBS (grade 1 within 2 weeks; grade 1–2 at 2–4 weeks) does not need IVIG/PLEX — but treat walking patients with fast decline, bulbar, or autonomic problems
Dysautonomia: exaggerated responses to vasoactive drugs; bradyarrhythmia with suctioning
escalateWhen: Ward → ICU: FVC <60% predicted, SBC <20, autonomic instability, worsening bulbar/neck weakness, or mEGRIS ≥23 (EAN/PNS 2023 Fig. 2)
FVC fall >30% in 24 h → immediate ICU transfer; 50% fall in <24 h → likely needs ventilation
In ICU: FVC <20 mL/kg, MEP <30 cmH2O, MIP <40 cmH2O, or FVC >30% below baseline → consider elective intubation before FVC ≤10 mL/kg
Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration, or FVC ≤10 mL/kg → intubate

PLEX machine type (continuous vs discontinuous flow) and line access

entries.title: Acute neuromuscular respiratory failure (undifferentiated)
keyNumbers: 20/30/40 rule (GBS cohort): VC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O predict need for ventilation (Lawn 2001)
EAN/PNS 2023 (GBS): consider elective ventilation at FVC ≤20 mL/kg, MEP <30 cmH2O, or MIP <40 cmH2O; SBC <20 → ICU
Michigan: MDHHS 517-335-8165 (office hours); 517-335-9030 (after hours)
Poison Control 1-800-222-1222
presentation: Dyspnea, orthopnea, tachypnea, paradoxical abdominal breathing, staccato speech, weak cough
Bulbar and neck flexor weakness; hypoxemia and hypercapnia are late
Localize: anterior horn (ALS, West Nile), nerve (GBS, CIP), NMJ (MG, LEMS, botulism, organophosphate, hypermagnesemia), muscle (myositis, rhabdo, hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia, periodic paralysis)
definitions: 20/30/40 rule (GBS cohort): VC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O predict need for ventilation (Lawn 2001)
EAN/PNS 2023 (GBS): consider elective ventilation at FVC ≤20 mL/kg, MEP <30 cmH2O, or MIP <40 cmH2O; SBC <20 → ICU

immediateActions.action: FVC (seated and supine if possible), NIF/MIP, single breath count, cough, secretions, neck flexion; gas if concern
Decide on the airway early: worsening bulbar function, can't clear secretions, or rapidly falling FVC → elective intubation, not a crash airway
Avoid succinylcholine with denervation, prolonged immobility, or rhabdomyolysis (hyperkalemia); MG: resistant to succinylcholine, very sensitive to nondepolarizers
Check K, Mg, phos, Ca, CK; search scalp, ears, and groin for a tick; review drugs and toxins; ask about home-canned food, injection drug use, wounds
Call the state health department now for consultation and antitoxin (BAT) — Michigan: MDHHS 517-335-8165 (office hours) or 517-335-9030 (after hours). Don't wait for lab confirmation (CDC 2021)
Atropine ± pralidoxime per toxicology; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222

workup.test: BMP with K, Mg, phos, Ca; CK; TSH

notes: Aspiration; diaphragm elevation

workup.test: Serum (± stool, wound, food) for botulinum toxin
notes: Draw serum BEFORE antitoxin; coordinate with health dept/CDC
Distinguishes nerve vs NMJ (incl. pre-synaptic: botulism, LEMS) vs muscle
Central causes of hypoventilation

treatment.agent: Airway: elective intubation (NIV only in selected NMJ cases)
treatment.doseText: N/A — see escalateWhen thresholds
notes: Facial weakness gives falsely low FVC (poor seal) — use a face mask

treatment.doseText: Dose per CDC/health department consult; released only via state health department → CDC
notes: No routine skin testing; have epinephrine and antihistamines at bedside
Halts progression, does not reverse existing paralysis

treatment.doseText: N/A — grasp close to skin, remove intact
notes: Improvement usually within hours to days after removal

treatment.doseText: Per institutional electrolyte protocol; IV calcium for symptomatic hypermagnesemia

pitfalls: Pure ventilatory pump failure: SpO2 normal until late — don't be reassured
Supine FVC drop suggests diaphragm weakness
Descending weakness + bulbar/ocular signs + preserved sensation + afebrile → think botulism
ICU patient failing to wean → critical illness polyneuropathy/myopathy
Severe respiratory weakness with mild limb weakness → MG, botulism, ALS, acid maltase deficiency, myopathy rather than GBS
escalateWhen: FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP/NIF weaker than −30 to −40 cmH2O, MEP <30–40 cmH2O (thresholds differ by source — see definitions)
Rising PaCO2 or acidosis; can't clear secretions; rapid FVC decline
Suspected botulism → health department call immediately

entries.title: Autoimmune encephalitis (incl. paraneoplastic)
keyNumbers: Methylprednisolone: 1 g IV daily ×3–7 days, then bridging therapy
IVIG: 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days
Plasma exchange (PLEX): 5–10 exchanges, every other day
Rituximab: 375 mg/m² weekly ×4, OR 1000 mg ×2 doses 2 weeks apart
Cyclophosphamide: 600–1000 mg/m² (per neuroimmunology/oncology)
presentation: Subacute (<3 months) working-memory loss, altered mental status, or psychiatric symptoms
Seizures (often new and refractory), focal CNS signs, movement disorders, autonomic instability, central hypoventilation
NMDAR phenotype: psychiatric/behavioral onset → speech change, seizures, dyskinesias, decreased consciousness, dysautonomia
Relapse weeks after treated HSV encephalitis can be post-HSV autoimmune (often NMDAR) encephalitis
definitions: Possible AE (Graus 2016) — all 3: (1) subacute onset <3 mo of working-memory deficit, altered mental status, or psychiatric symptoms; (2) ≥1 of: new focal CNS findings, unexplained seizures, CSF WBC >5/mm³, MRI suggestive of encephalitis; (3) reasonable exclusion of alternatives

Definite autoimmune limbic encephalitis (Graus 2016) — all 4: subacute limbic syndrome; bilateral medial temporal T2/FLAIR abnormality; CSF WBC >5/mm³ or temporal EEG epileptic/slow activity; reasonable exclusion. If one of the first 3 is missing, definite LE requires an antibody

Probable anti-NMDAR (Graus 2016): ≥4 of 6 symptom groups (behavior/cognition, speech, seizures, movement disorder, ↓consciousness, autonomic/hypoventilation) + abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis/OCB + exclusion; or 3 groups + systemic teratoma
Definite anti-NMDAR: ≥1 symptom group + IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies (CSF testing required) after exclusion of other disorders

PNS-Care 2021: high-risk antibodies >70% cancer association; intermediate-risk 30–70%. High-risk phenotypes: encephalomyelitis, limbic encephalitis, rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome, opsoclonus-myoclonus, sensory neuronopathy, GI pseudo-obstruction, LEMS

immediateActions.action: Treat as infection until excluded: empiric acyclovir ± bacterial meningitis coverage
MRI brain with/without contrast; LP; EEG (cEEG if fluctuating or seizing)
Send PAIRED serum + CSF neural antibody panels, ideally before IVIG/PLEX

immediateActions.window: Infection reasonably excluded (CSF cells, glucose, Gram stain, viral PCR)
immediateActions.action: Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for antibodies — unless biopsy for lymphoma/neurosarcoid is being considered
Tumor screen: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast; pelvic/testicular US for NMDAR phenotype; if negative: mammogram/breast MRI, pelvic US, FDG-PET

immediateActions.window: End of first cycle, no improvement
immediateActions.action: Add IVIG or PLEX

immediateActions.window: 2–4 wk of optimized first-line, no improvement
immediateActions.action: Second-line: rituximab (antibody-mediated) or cyclophosphamide (cell-mediated/classic paraneoplastic)

notes: Normal in many antibody-positive cases

workup.test: LP: cells, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture, HSV/VZV PCR, OCB, IgG index; cytology/flow if lymphoma possible
Paired serum + CSF autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels
notes: CSF more sensitive for NMDAR, GFAP; serum more sensitive for LGI1, AQP4 (Abboud 2021)
Cell-surface antibody in serum only (CSF negative) → confirm before calling definite (PNS-Care)
Extreme delta brush supports NMDAR
Hyponatremia is common in LGI1 encephalitis
Repeat every 4–6 months for 2 years if high-risk phenotype + high-risk antibody and initial screen negative (PNS-Care)

indication: Initial CT negative and paraneoplastic suspicion persists

workup.test: HIV, syphilis, TSH/TPO antibodies, B12, ammonia, toxicology
notes: Mimic exclusion

treatment.doseText: 1 g IV daily ×3–7 days, then bridging therapy
notes: 84% of surveyed experts chose steroids alone or combined as first-line for a general AE presentation
Bridging after discharge (survey): oral prednisone taper most common (38%), then periodic IVIG (28%), rituximab ± prednisone (16%), weekly/monthly IVMP (12%)
Prolonged steroids: PPI, vitamin D, PJP prophylaxis when indicated; control BP and glucose
evidenceNote: Abboud 2021 (AEA Clinicians Network best-practice recommendations; survey + literature)
Abboud 2021 long-term management companion paper (bridging survey)

treatment.doseText: 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days
notes: Consider IVIG first in agitated patients and bleeding disorders
Draw antibodies before IVIG

treatment.doseText: 5–10 exchanges, every other day
notes: Consider PLEX first with severe hyponatremia, high thromboembolic or cancer risk, or associated demyelination
Don't give PLEX right after IVIG

treatment.doseText: 375 mg/m² weekly ×4, OR 1000 mg ×2 doses 2 weeks apart
notes: Preferred for suspected antibody-mediated (cell-surface) disease
Screen HBV before
evidenceNote: Abboud 2021: 80% of responders chose rituximab as second-line with unknown antibody

treatment.doseText: 600–1000 mg/m² (per neuroimmunology/oncology)
notes: Favored for suspected cell-mediated disease (classic paraneoplastic, intracellular antibodies)

treatment.doseText: N/A — surgical/oncologic
notes: Tumor removal is part of immunotherapy response in paraneoplastic disease

pitfalls: Graus 'possible AE' is an entry point, not a diagnosis — specificity was 27% in a real-world validation (mimics common)
LGI1: CSF pleocytosis in only ~41% and MRI may be normal; antibody best detected in serum
NMDAR: test CSF — serum-only testing risks false negatives and positives
IVIG/PLEX before sampling can mask antibodies
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures (LGI1) respond poorly to ASMs — immunotherapy is the treatment
Steroids before biopsy can obscure CNS lymphoma
escalateWhen: Refractory seizures or NORSE → see refractory-super-refractory-se
Central hypoventilation, autonomic storm, or declining consciousness (NMDAR) → ICU
No response after first-line + IVIG/PLEX → neuroimmunology for second-line

Rituximab/cyclophosphamide inpatient access and HBV screening workflow

entries.title: Bacterial meningitis (community-acquired & post-neurosurgical, adult)
keyNumbers: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h, started 10–20 min before or with the first antibiotic dose (IDSA A-I)
Vancomycin: 30–45 mg/kg/day divided q8–12h (IDSA 2004); load and monitor per institutional AUC/trough protocol
Ceftriaxone: 2 g IV q12h (IDSA adult total 4 g/day, interval q12–24h)
Ampicillin (Listeria coverage): 2 g IV q4h (12 g/day) — add if age >50, immunocompromised, or alcohol use disorder
Acyclovir: 10 mg/kg IV q8h until HSV excluded — see viral-encephalitis
presentation: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status — classic triad often incomplete
Petechial/purpuric rash → meningococcus
Older, immunocompromised, or alcohol use → Listeria risk
Recent neurosurgery, shunt, EVD, or penetrating trauma → staphylococci, C. acnes (P. acnes), and gram-negative rods
definitions: IDSA CT-before-LP criteria (any): immunocompromise (HIV, immunosuppressants, transplant); history of CNS disease (mass, stroke, focal infection); new-onset seizure within 1 week; papilledema; abnormal level of consciousness; focal neurologic deficit (B-II)
Typical bacterial CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low CSF glucose / low CSF:serum ratio, high protein, elevated opening pressure

EVD/shunt CSF culture (IDSA 2017): contamination = single positive culture or Gram stain, normal CSF cells/glucose/protein, no symptoms; colonization = multiple positives, normal CSF, no symptoms; infection = ≥1 positive culture + pleocytosis and/or low glucose or rising cell count + symptoms (Rec 22: strong, high)
After neurosurgery or head trauma: CoNS in enrichment broth only or on 1 of multiple cultures, normal CSF, no fever → not infection (IDSA 2017 Rec 26: strong, low)

After neurosurgery, infection (vs chemical meningitis) more likely if CSF WBC >7500/mm³ or CSF glucose <10 mg/dL; fever ≥40 °C or >1 week more suggestive in one study. No single variable reliably separates them (IDSA 2017 evidence summary, ungraded)

immediateActions.action: Blood cultures ×2 — then give dexamethasone and antibiotics; do NOT wait for CT or LP
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h, started 10–20 min before or with the first antibiotic dose (IDSA A-I)
CT before LP only if IDSA criteria met — antibiotics go in before the patient leaves for CT
Opening pressure, cell count/diff, glucose (paired serum), protein, Gram stain, culture; multiplex PCR if available; save extra CSF
Continue dexamethasone only if Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci or blood/CSF grows S. pneumoniae; otherwise stop. Narrow antibiotics to organism
Droplet precautions; notify public health for contact prophylaxis

notes: Before antibiotics
VA shunt: recommended — bacteremia in >90% of infected VA shunts (IDSA 2017 Rec 20: strong, high); VP or ventriculopleural shunt: may be considered (Rec 21: weak, low)
Most head CTs before LP don't change management — only 1.5% did in one cohort (CID 2017)
CSF culture yield falls within hours of antibiotics; cell profile persists

indication: Pretreated with antibiotics or Gram stain negative

notes: If initial cultures negative: hold ≥10 days for C. acnes (IDSA 2017 Rec 17: strong, high)

indication: Suspected post-neurosurgical, shunt, or EVD meningitis
notes: May help diagnose (IDSA 2017 Rec 30: weak, moderate)
Study data (ungraded): CSF lactate cutoff 4 mmol/L after neurosurgery — sensitivity 88%, specificity 98% (LP within 40 days of surgery)
SAH and brain injury raise CSF lactate; shunt infection: lactate normal in ~20%, and a 4 mmol/L cutoff missed almost half in one series
Study data (ungraded): CSF procalcitonin 0.075 ng/mL + CSF lactate 3.45 mmol/L combined — sensitivity 96%, NPV 97.6% (one small study)
May help diagnose (IDSA 2017 Rec 33: strong, moderate); a negative culture does not exclude fungal infection
Study data (ungraded): CSF β-D-glucan ≥80 pg/mL (manufacturer cutoff) — sensitivity 96%, specificity 95% in the 2012 contaminated-methylprednisolone outbreak

treatment.doseText: 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h ×2–4 days; first dose 10–20 min before or with the first antibiotic. Many adult protocols use 10 mg q6h ×4 days (de Gans 2002 regimen)
notes: IDSA: give for suspected or proven pneumococcal meningitis; many give to all adults since etiology is unknown at presentation (B-III)
Do NOT start if antibiotics already given — unlikely to help (A-I)
Some experts add rifampin when dexamethasone is used (B-III), given reduced CSF vancomycin penetration concerns

treatment.doseText: 30–45 mg/kg/day divided q8–12h (IDSA 2004); load and monitor per institutional AUC/trough protocol
notes: Covers resistant pneumococcus pending susceptibilities
evidenceNote: IDSA 2004 Table 4 (A-III); adult dose 30–45 mg/kg/day q8–12h (dosing table)

treatment.doseText: 2 g IV q12h (IDSA adult total 4 g/day, interval q12–24h)
notes: Cefotaxime 8–12 g/day divided q4–6h is the IDSA alternative

treatment.doseText: 2 g IV q4h (12 g/day) — add if age >50, immunocompromised, or alcohol use disorder
notes: IDSA empiric indication: age >50 (Table 4); many also add for immunocompromise, pregnancy, or alcohol use disorder
Listeria alternatives: TMP-SMX or meropenem (B-III)

treatment.agent: Post-neurosurgery / penetrating trauma / CSF shunt or drain: vancomycin + cefepime, ceftazidime, or meropenem
treatment.doseText: Vancomycin 30–60 mg/kg/day divided q8–12h (trough 15–20 μg/mL if intermittent bolus) + one of: cefepime 2 g q8h, ceftazidime 2 g q8h, or meropenem 2 g q8h; choose the beta-lactam by local susceptibility
notes: Pseudomonas coverage required
Infected EVD: remove. Infected shunt: remove completely, replace with EVD + IV antibiotics (IDSA 2017 Recs 62–63: strong, moderate)

Duration: CoNS or C. acnes with no/minimal pleocytosis, normal glucose, few symptoms: 10 days; with significant pleocytosis, low glucose, or symptoms: 10–14 days; S. aureus or gram-negative bacilli: 10–14 days (some experts 21 days for gram-negative, weak, low); repeatedly positive cultures: 10–14 days after the last positive (IDSA 2017 Recs 58–61: strong, low)
evidenceNote: IDSA 2017 Rec 37: strong, low; Rec 38 (vancomycin trough): strong, low; adult doses Table 2

treatment.doseText: Intraventricular via EVD, preservative-free; clamp drain 15–60 min. Adult vancomycin 5 mg (slit ventricles), 10 mg (normal), 15–20 mg (enlarged); gentamicin 2 / 3 / 4–5 mg. Interval by EVD output per 24 h: <50 mL every 3rd day; 50–100 mL every 2nd day; 100–150 mL daily; 150–200 mL add 5 mg vancomycin / 1 mg gentamicin, daily; 200–250 mL add 10 mg / 2 mg, daily
notes: Consider only when infection responds poorly to IV therapy alone (Rec 55: strong, low)
Adjust dose and interval to CSF concentration 10–20× the organism's MIC, ventricle size, and EVD output (Rec 57: strong, low)
No intraventricular/intrathecal penicillins or cephalosporins — neurotoxicity, especially seizures
Not FDA-approved by this route; dosing is empiric and not validated
evidenceNote: IDSA 2017 Recs 55–57: strong, low; clamp time Rec 56; doses Table 3

treatment.doseText: Per ID: vancomycin + moxifloxacin 400 mg IV q24h (IDSA alternative); add TMP-SMX for Listeria if indicated; aztreonam or ciprofloxacin as gram-negative alternatives
10 mg/kg IV q8h until HSV excluded — see viral-encephalitis
600 mg q24h (IDSA adult dose) — consider with dexamethasone or for ceftriaxone-nonsusceptible pneumococcus
notes: Never as monotherapy

Staphylococcal infection with a CSF shunt, drain, or other intracranial/spinal hardware, rifampin-susceptible isolate: add as part of combination therapy (IDSA 2017 Rec 44: strong, low; adult 600 mg q24h, Table 2)

pitfalls: Never delay antibiotics for imaging or LP
Avoid piperacillin-tazobactam — poor CNS penetration
CSF can sterilize within hours of antibiotics — blood cultures first, multiplex PCR helps
Over-use of CT before LP delays treatment; apply the IDSA criteria

EVD not being used to treat a shunt infection: no routine daily CSF cultures/analysis unless clinically indicated (IDSA 2017 Rec 69: strong, low). Infected, with an EVD: repeat CSF cultures until negative (Rec 67: strong, low)
escalateWhen: Altered consciousness, seizures, shock, or rising ICP → ICU
Hydrocephalus, abscess, or empyema on imaging → neurosurgery
No clinical improvement at 48 h → repeat LP/imaging, reconsider organism/resistance
institutionVaries: Vancomycin dosing protocol (AUC vs trough)
Local pneumococcal resistance (antibiogram)
CSF multiplex PCR availability

Acyclovir (VZV): 10–15 mg/kg IV q8h ×10–14 days

Overused acute drugs (ergots, triptans, opioids ≥10 days/month) can cause medication-overuse headache (DHE label); Nagy stopped all overuse on admission and started preventives ~1 week after discharge
Not on card (US availability not addressed in sources): dexketoprofen, IV acetylsalicylic acid, IM diclofenac, lysine clonixinate; dipyrone is withdrawn from the US (AHS 2016)
escalateWhen: Attack differs from the patient's usual migraine, new focal deficit, or no response — reconsider a secondary cause (ICHD-3: not better accounted for by another diagnosis)
Chest pain or signs of vasoconstriction on DHE → stop DHE, ECG and evaluate before further doses (label)

entries.title: Neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis (adult)
keyNumbers: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G: 18–24 million units/day as 3–4 million units IV q4h or continuous infusion × 10–14 days
Procaine penicillin G + probenecid: 2.4 million units IM once daily + 500 mg PO 4 times/day, both × 10–14 days — only if adherence can be ensured
Ceftriaxone (penicillin allergy): 1–2 g IV or IM daily × 10–14 days
HIV: CSF WBC >5/mm³ can reflect HIV alone; a >20/mm³ cutoff may improve neurosyphilis specificity
Fourfold titer change (2 dilutions, e.g., 1:16 → 1:4) is significant; use the same test (RPR and VDRL titers not interchangeable; RPR often slightly higher), ideally the same lab
presentation: Early neurosyphilis (first months–years): cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, meningovascular syphilis, stroke, acute altered mental status; late (10 to >30 years): tabes dorsalis, general paresis — CNS involvement can occur at any stage

Ocular syphilis: often panuveitis; also conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, posterior interstitial keratitis, optic neuropathy, retinal vasculitis, neuroretinitis — any stage, with or without CNS involvement; can cause permanent vision loss
Otosyphilis: tinnitus, vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss — unilateral or bilateral, can be sudden and progress rapidly; can be permanent
definitions: Serologic diagnosis needs both a nontreponemal (RPR/VDRL) and a treponemal test (TP-PA, EIA/CIA, FTA-ABS); either alone can misclassify

Reverse algorithm (EIA/CIA first): reactive → reflex quantitative RPR; RPR nonreactive → second treponemal test (TP-PA preferred). TP-PA reactive: previously treated → nothing more unless re-exposure; untreated → treat as late latent / unknown duration. TP-PA nonreactive + low risk → no further workup or treatment
Fourfold titer change (2 dilutions, e.g., 1:16 → 1:4) is significant; use the same test (RPR and VDRL titers not interchangeable; RPR often slightly higher), ideally the same lab
Neurosyphilis diagnosis = CSF tests (cell count, protein, CSF-VDRL) + reactive serum nontreponemal and treponemal tests + neurologic signs or symptoms; no single test is diagnostic in all cases
CSF-VDRL: highly specific, insensitive; the only FDA-cleared CSF test. Reactive CSF-VDRL (no blood contamination) + neurologic signs or symptoms = diagnostic

CSF-VDRL negative but neurologic signs, reactive serology, and lymphocytic pleocytosis or high protein → neurosyphilis still possible: send CSF FTA-ABS (highly sensitive, less specific). Negative CSF FTA-ABS makes neurosyphilis highly unlikely
CSF TP-PA: CDC 2021 — sensitivity and specificity appear similar to CSF FTA-ABS; CDC 2024 lab — more data needed before it can be recommended off-label
HIV: CSF WBC >5/mm³ can reflect HIV alone; a >20/mm³ cutoff may improve neurosyphilis specificity
Ocular and otic syphilis: CSF-VDRL sensitivity <50% (ocular) and <10% (otic); no CSF treponemal test is recommended without neurologic signs

Penicillin allergy, low-risk history: GI symptoms, headache, pruritus without rash, localized rash, delayed rash (>24 h), symptoms unknown, family history only, or on the record but denied → amoxicillin oral challenge can document no allergy; 3rd-generation cephalosporins are often given without testing

Penicillin allergy, high-risk history: anaphylaxis within 6 h of a dose (within the past 10 years), SJS/TEN/DRESS/AGEP, or other severe non-IgE reactions (kidney or liver injury, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia) → no β-lactam, skin test or challenge in an ambulatory setting; allergist. After SJS/TEN or other severe non-IgE reactions: not a candidate for skin test or challenge; avoid penicillin and all β-lactams indefinitely

No neurologic, ocular or otic findings (or normal CSF): treat by stage — primary, secondary, early latent: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM ×1; late latent / unknown duration, or tertiary with normal CSF: 2.4 million units IM weekly ×3 (7.2 million units total)

immediateActions.action: Reactive serology + cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, stroke, acute or chronic altered mental status, cognitive dysfunction, motor or sensory deficit, or loss of vibration sense → LP before treatment

Full ocular exam incl. cranial nerves; urgent ophthalmology. Cranial nerve dysfunction → LP. Isolated ocular findings confirmed on exam → no LP needed; treat as neurosyphilis even if CSF is normal. Symptoms but normal eye exam → LP may help
Normal neuro exam → no LP (CSF likely normal; doesn't change management); otologic exam, ENT; treat as neurosyphilis
HIV test; offer HIV PrEP if negative
Report to the local or state health department (provider and/or lab, per state law)

workup.test: Quantitative serum RPR or VDRL (endpoint titer) + treponemal test
notes: Baseline titer for follow-up — use the same test type afterwards
Nonreactive undiluted test despite signs of syphilis → ask the lab to rule out prozone (dilution series)

indication: Ocular syphilis with cranial nerve dysfunction or other neurologic findings
Ocular symptoms with a normal eye exam (may help)
Suspected treatment failure (≥4-fold titer rise or recurrent signs) with neurologic findings or no recent sexual exposure
notes: Avoid blood contamination — causes false-positive CSF tests
Not routine in primary, secondary or latent syphilis without neurologic, ocular or otic findings, with or without HIV

indication: CSF-VDRL negative with neurologic signs, reactive serology, and pleocytosis or high protein
notes: Off-label; send to a lab experienced with CSF testing
Value is the negative result; a positive result is not diagnostic
HIV and syphilis: thorough neurologic, ocular and otic exam; CSF only if the neurologic exam is abnormal

workup.test: Follow-up serum RPR or VDRL (same test as baseline)
notes: Serum RPR normalization predicts CSF normalization — repeat LP unnecessary with serologic and clinical response (HIV-negative, or HIV on ART)
HIV: CSF parameters may normalize more slowly, especially with advanced immunosuppression
Persistent or recurrent signs, or ≥4-fold titer rise sustained >2 weeks → reinfection or treatment failure: re-evaluate (CSF if neurologic findings) and retest HIV

treatment.doseText: 18–24 million units/day as 3–4 million units IV q4h or continuous infusion × 10–14 days
notes: Same regimen for ocular syphilis (even if CSF is normal) and otosyphilis
Same regimen with HIV
Pregnancy: penicillin only — desensitize if allergic
evidenceNote: CDC 2021: Recommended Regimen (p.46); no grade assigned
Ocular: "treated similarly to neurosyphilis, even if a CSF examination is normal"; otic: "same regimen as for neurosyphilis" (p.46); HIV p.49; pregnancy p.47

treatment.doseText: 2.4 million units IM once daily + 500 mg PO 4 times/day, both × 10–14 days — only if adherence can be ensured
evidenceNote: CDC 2021: Alternative Regimen, "if compliance with therapy can be ensured" (p.46); no grade assigned

treatment.doseText: 1–2 g IV or IM daily × 10–14 days
notes: Cross-reactivity of 3rd-generation cephalosporins in IgE-mediated penicillin allergy <1% (CDC: negligible)
If concern about ceftriaxone safety: penicillin skin test, then desensitization with a specialist if positive
Pregnancy: not an option — data insufficient; desensitize to penicillin
HIV: same option (small observational studies, 1–2 g IV daily × 10–14 days)
evidenceNote: CDC 2021: "Limited data indicate" ceftriaxone "can be used as an alternative" (p.47); HIV p.49; no grade assigned

treatment.agent: Benzathine penicillin G after the IV or procaine course
treatment.doseText: 2.4 million units IM weekly × 1–3 weeks after completing the neurosyphilis regimen — can be considered, for a total duration comparable to latent syphilis treatment
notes: Never the neurosyphilis treatment by itself
evidenceNote: CDC 2021: "can be considered" (p.46); no grade assigned

treatment.agent: Penicillin allergy: skin test → amoxicillin challenge → desensitization
treatment.doseText: Skin test (major + minor determinants); if negative, observed amoxicillin 250 mg PO challenge (1 h observation), then penicillin. Positive skin test and no alternative → allergist desensitization in a monitored inpatient setting
notes: Desensitization is required when penicillin allergy is documented and no alternative exists (e.g., pregnancy, neurosyphilis)
No antihistamines within 7 days before skin testing
Skin testing in pregnancy is considered safe; oral challenge only where support services are available
High-risk history (see definitions) → no skin test or challenge; allergist
evidenceNote: CDC 2021: Management of Persons Who Have a History of Penicillin Allergy, pp.57–59 (validation steps p.57; allergist, monitored inpatient p.58; antihistamines, pregnancy, desensitization p.59); no grade assigned

pitfalls: Benzathine penicillin alone is not a neurosyphilis regimen (poor CNS levels); Bicillin C-R (benzathine + procaine) is not appropriate for any stage — check the product name

Fever, headache, myalgia within 24 h of starting therapy = Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, not penicillin allergy; antipyretics treat symptoms but don't prevent it. In pregnancy it can trigger labor — don't delay treatment
Systemic steroids are often used for ocular and otic syphilis but are not proven beneficial
Treponemal tests stay reactive for life in most (15–25% treated in the primary stage revert); don't use treponemal titers to judge response
CSF abnormalities are common in early syphilis without neurologic findings and have unknown significance — no routine LP
HIV: CD4 ≤350 or RPR ≥1:32 is linked to CSF abnormalities, but LP-guided treatment without neurologic signs hasn't improved outcomes — LP only for an abnormal neuro exam
A reactive CSF FTA-ABS doesn't confirm neurosyphilis: specificity 55–100% in syphilis without symptomatic neurosyphilis (serum antibody crossing an inflamed blood–brain barrier)
escalateWhen: Suspected ocular syphilis → immediate ophthalmology referral and co-management
Otosyphilis → co-manage with ENT
Positive penicillin skin test, or high-risk allergy history → allergist (desensitization) + ID; no other neurosyphilis regimen is adequately evaluated
Pregnancy → penicillin only (desensitize if allergic); involve obstetrics
Tertiary or cardiovascular syphilis → ID (some treat all cardiovascular syphilis with a neurosyphilis regimen)
Complex titer interpretation → STD Clinical Consultation Network (stdccn.org)
institutionVaries: Lab serology algorithm (traditional vs reverse) and whether CSF FTA-ABS is sent out
Benzathine penicillin G (Bicillin L-A) availability — check pharmacy and current shortage notices
Penicillin skin testing / allergy service availability
Health department reporting and partner services (Michigan)

entries.title: Lyme neuroborreliosis (adult)
keyNumbers: Ceftriaxone: 2000 mg IV once daily × 14–21 days
Doxycycline: 100 mg PO twice daily or 200 mg once daily × 14–21 days
Parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement: IV over oral; typically 2–4-week courses (duration never studied)
Lyme vs enteroviral meningitis: Lyme more likely with facial nerve palsy, symptoms >7 days, and mononuclear-predominant CSF pleocytosis

CSF:serum antibody index: elevated = highly specific for CNS Lyme; sensitivity >85% in 2 small US meningitis studies, 56–79% in European early neuroborreliosis; a normal index does not exclude; may stay elevated for years after successful treatment
presentation: Early (first few months of infection; onset over hours to days): meningitis, cranial neuritis, radiculoneuritis; rarely encephalomyelitis. Later: PNS or CNS involvement with a more indolent course
Cranial neuropathy: VII most common; also VIII, less commonly III, V, VI
PNS: painful radiculoneuritis, plexopathy, mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex (incl. confluent)
Raised ICP with papilledema (pseudotumor-like), even without other signs of meningitis — almost all reported cases are children; can compromise vision
Parenchymal brain or spinal cord disease (focal exam or MRI findings): exceedingly rare; cord involvement typically with painful radiculitis at related segments
definitions: Test for Lyme (strong, moderate): acute meningitis, painful radiculoneuritis, mononeuropathy multiplex, acute cranial neuropathy, or spinal cord (rarely brain) inflammation — with epidemiologically plausible tick exposure
Don't test routinely (strong, low): typical ALS, relapsing-remitting MS, Parkinson's disease, dementia or cognitive decline, new-onset seizures, psychiatric illness
Other neurologic syndromes without clinical or epidemiologic support for Lyme: don't screen (strong, low). Nonspecific brain MRI white matter abnormalities alone: suggest against testing (weak, low)
Serum antibody by 2-tier testing (EIA/IFA then IgM + IgG immunoblots, or modified 2-tier with two EIAs) is the test for PNS or CNS disease — not PCR or culture of CSF or serum (strong, moderate)
If CSF is tested: paired CSF + serum for the CSF:serum antibody index at a lab with a validated method; no CSF serology without the index; no routine CSF PCR or culture (strong, moderate)

CSF:serum antibody index: elevated = highly specific for CNS Lyme; sensitivity >85% in 2 small US meningitis studies, 56–79% in European early neuroborreliosis; a normal index does not exclude; may stay elevated for years after successful treatment
CSF PCR sensitivity: 17% (meta-analysis, acute neuroborreliosis), 5% (US Lyme meningitis); blood PCR or culture 1–28%
Active CNS (not necessarily PNS) disease usually has a CSF lymphocytic/monocytic pleocytosis; CSF may be normal when disease is limited to the PNS
Seronegative at presentation (occasional in early neuroborreliosis): typically strongly seropositive on repeat testing several weeks later; rarely the index is positive before serum
IgG seronegativity in an untreated patient with months to years of symptoms essentially rules out Lyme disease
IgM and IgG can persist for years or decades after cure — seropositivity does not separate past from active infection
Lyme vs enteroviral meningitis: Lyme more likely with facial nerve palsy, symptoms >7 days, and mononuclear-predominant CSF pleocytosis
CSF CXCL13: not standardized, raised in other infectious, inflammatory and neoplastic conditions; not recommended. Falls rapidly with treatment

immediateActions.window: Meningitis or encephalitis, diagnosis not confirmed
immediateActions.action: Empiric IV regimen covering other bacterial and viral pathogens first; once those are excluded or Lyme is confirmed, oral doxycycline may be considered
Serum Lyme antibody (2-tier); if an LP is done, send paired CSF + serum for the antibody index

immediateActions.window: Acute facial palsy, Lyme not established (age ≥16)
immediateActions.action: Corticosteroids within 72 h of onset per facial palsy guidelines — don't wait for Lyme serology
Antibiotics. Steroids: no recommendation (knowledge gap) — stopping steroids already started, or starting them, is patient preference and clinical judgment
Lower ICP to prevent visual loss, regardless of etiology

notes: Modified 2-tier often detects early cases that are EIA-reactive but miss immunoblot criteria

workup.test: LP: opening pressure, cell count, paired CSF + serum Lyme antibody index
indication: Suspected meningitis — to exclude bacterial, viral or other causes
Baseline pleocytosis as a metric of treatment response
notes: Individualize — recommended treatment may be the same with or without meningitis
Herniation has never been reported in Lyme neuroborreliosis; LP risk relates to the other diagnoses under consideration

indication: Focal CNS findings on exam (suspected parenchymal disease)
notes: Rare contrast-enhancing parenchymal lesions; can mimic a first demyelinating episode
Nonspecific white matter abnormalities are no more common than in controls

treatment.doseText: 2000 mg IV once daily × 14–21 days
notes: Preferred IV agent
Parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement: IV over oral; typically 2–4-week courses (duration never studied)
Inpatient or ED, more acutely ill, or tolerating oral medication poorly: initial IV preferable
Route may be changed from IV to oral during treatment
evidenceNote: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 XIII.1: IV ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, penicillin G, or oral doxycycline over other antimicrobials — strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence (e27); dose Table 3, duration Table 4 with footnote d (e11)
XIV.1: IV over oral antibiotics for parenchymal involvement — strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence; "Typically, 2- to 4-week courses have been used successfully" (e28)

treatment.doseText: 100 mg PO twice daily or 200 mg once daily × 14–21 days
notes: For meningitis, cranial neuropathy, radiculoneuropathy and other PNS manifestations; not for parenchymal brain or spinal cord disease (IV)
Cranial nerve palsy: oral doxycycline is the only regimen listed
Oral vs IV equivalence comes from European trials (14-day courses, 200 mg/day); no high-quality US studies
The only well-studied oral option: azithromycin is not sufficiently studied beyond erythema migrans; amoxicillin and cefuroxime axetil have not been assessed directly
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: individualize against the alternatives
evidenceNote: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 XIII.1 — strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence (e27); dose Table 3, durations Table 4 (e11)
Evidence summary and rationale e27–e28; azithromycin Table 4 footnote c (e11); pregnancy e12

treatment.doseText: 2000 mg IV three times daily × 14–21 days
notes: May need dose adjustment in renal impairment
evidenceNote: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 XIII.1 — strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence (e27); Table 3 "Alternative" IV agent with footnote a; Table 4 footnote d (e11)

treatment.doseText: 18–24 million units/day IV divided every 4 hours × 14–21 days
notes: May need dose adjustment in renal impairment
evidenceNote: IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 XIII.1 — strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence (e27); Table 3 "Alternative" IV agent with footnote a; Table 4 footnote d (e11)

pitfalls: Steroids in Lyme-associated facial palsy: no recommendation — some studies suggest benefit, others possible harm; the evidence is small and methodologically limited

Persistent or recurring nonspecific symptoms (fatigue, pain, cognitive impairment) after recommended treatment, without objective reinfection or treatment failure (arthritis, meningitis, neuropathy): no additional antibiotics (strong, moderate)
Nonspecific T2 white matter hyperintensities are not useful for diagnosing neuroborreliosis — common with vascular risk factors, migraine and age
Lyme encephalopathy (concentration, memory, cognitive complaints) without focal CNS abnormalities on exam or imaging is generally not encephalitis
Courses longer than 21 days have not been shown more effective; 100 days of amoxicillin after 3 weeks of IV ceftriaxone did not improve response and raised adverse effects (RR 3.70)
Response may lag beyond the treatment course; CSF pleocytosis improves but takes an extended period to resolve completely
Symptom flare, with or without fever, in the first 24 h of antibiotics (Jarisch-Herxheimer-like): usually mild and self-limited; symptoms arising later in treatment are not this reaction
Immunoblots on paired serum and CSF, or on CSF alone, are not indicated outside research to assess intrathecal antibody production
escalateWhen: Focal CNS findings on exam or MRI evidence of brain or spinal cord involvement → IV therapy, not oral
Papilledema or raised ICP → lower ICP to prevent visual loss
Dyspnea, edema, palpitations, lightheadedness, chest pain or syncope → ECG; PR >300 ms, other arrhythmias or myopericarditis → admit with continuous ECG monitoring
Objective signs of relapse after treatment (e.g., meningitis, neuropathy) → a second course may be needed
institutionVaries: Lab's Lyme serology algorithm (standard vs modified 2-tier) and access to a validated CSF:serum antibody index
Cefotaxime and IV penicillin G availability
Outpatient IV antibiotic arrangements if an IV course continues after discharge
Health department reporting (Michigan)
